dotted-tail notationprocedurefor procedure parameters definedottedwith dotted-tail notation argument(s)arbitrary number of procedurearbitrary number of arguments The procedures +, *, and list take arbitrary numbers of arguments. One way to define such procedures is to use define with dotted-tail notation. In a procedure definition, a parameter list that has a dot before the last parameter name indicates that, when the procedure is called, the initial parameters (if any) will have as values the initial arguments, as usual, but the final parameters value will be a list of any remaining arguments. For instance, given the definition
(define (f x y . z) $\langle \textit{body} \rangle$)
the procedure f can be called with two or more arguments. If we evaluate
(f 1 2 3 4 5 6)
then in the body of f, x will be 1, y will be 2, and z will be the list (3 4 5 6). Given the definition
(define (g . w) $\langle \textit{body} \rangle$)
the procedure g can be called with zero or more arguments. If we evaluate
(g 1 2 3 4 5 6)
then in the body of g, w will be the list (1 2 3 4 5 6).To define f and g using lambdadottedwith dotted-tail notation lambda we would write
(define f (lambda (x y . z) body)) (define g (lambda w body))

One extremely useful operation is to apply some transformation to each element in a list and generate the list of results. For instance, the following
procedure function
scales each number in a list by a given factor:
BILINGUAL.JA:
非常に便利な操作の一つは、リストの各要素に何らかの変換を適用して結果のリストを生成することです。たとえば、次の
手続き 関数
はリスト内の各数に与えられた係数を掛けます：

SNIPPET.NAME: scale_list
SNIPPET.SCHEME: (define (scale-list items factor) (if (null? items) nil (cons (* (car items) factor) (scale-list (cdr items) factor))))

BILINGUAL.EN:

SCHEME.FOOTNOTE:
Scheme standardly provides a mapwith multiple arguments map procedure that is more general than the one described here. This more general map takes a procedure of $n$ arguments, together with $n$ lists, and applies the procedure to all the first elements of the lists, all the second elements of the lists, and so on, returning a list of the results. For example:
general_map_example general_map plus
(map + (list 1 2 3) (list 40 50 60) (list 700 800 900))
(741 852 963)
general_map_example2 general_map
(map (lambda (x y) (+ x (* 2 y))) (list 1 2 3) (list 4 5 6))

SNIPPET.NAME: map
SNIPPET.SCHEME: (define (map proc items) (if (null? items) nil (cons (proc (car items)) (map proc (cdr items)))))

BILINGUAL.EN:
Map The function map
is an important construct, not only because it captures a common pattern, but because it establishes a higher level of abstraction in dealing with lists. In the original definition of
scale-list, scale_list,
the recursive structure of the program draws attention to the element-by-element processing of the list. Defining
scale-list scale_list
in terms of map suppresses that level of detail and emphasizes that scaling transforms a list of elements to a list of results. The difference between the two definitions is not that the computer is performing a different process (it isnt) but that we think about the process differently. In effect, map helps establish an abstraction barrier that isolates the implementation of
procedures functions
that transform lists from the details of how the elements of the list are extracted and combined. Like the barriers shown in
figure,
figure,
this abstraction gives us the flexibility to change the low-level details of how sequences are implemented, while preserving the conceptual framework of operations that transform sequences to sequences. Section expands on this use of sequences as a framework for organizing programs.
BILINGUAL.JA:
map 関数 map
は重要な構成要素です。共通パターンを捉えるだけでなく、リストを扱う際のより高い抽象レベルを確立するからです。
scale-list scale_list
の元の定義では、プログラムの再帰的構造がリストの要素ごとの処理に注意を向けさせます。 map を使って
scale-list scale_list
を定義すると、その詳細レベルが抑制され、スケーリングが要素のリストを結果のリストに変換することが強調されます。2つの定義の違いは、コンピュータが異なるプロセスを実行していること（実行していません）ではなく、プロセスについて異なる考え方をしていることです。実際、map はリストを変換する
手続き 関数
の実装を、リストの要素がどのように取り出され組み合わされるかの詳細から分離する抽象バリアを確立するのに役立ちます。

BILINGUAL.EN:
Louis then tries to fix his bug by interchanging the arguments to
cons: pair:

SNIPPET.NAME: square_list3
SNIPPET.SCHEME: (define (square-list items) (define (iter things answer) (if (null? things) answer (iter (cdr things) (cons answer (square (car things)))))) (iter items nil))

BILINGUAL.EN: This doesnt work either. Explain.
BILINGUAL.JA: これもうまくいきません。その理由を説明してください。

BILINGUAL.EN:
The result list is reversed in the first program because the argument list is traversed in the given order, from first to last, but squares are added successively to the front of the answer list via cons. pair.
The last element of the list is the last one to be added to the answer and thus ends up as the first element of the result list.
BILINGUAL.JA:
最初のプログラムで結果リストが逆順になるのは、引数リストが先頭から末尾へと与えられた順序で走査されるのに対し、二乗は cons pair
によって結果リストの先頭に順次追加されるためです。リストの最後の要素が最後に追加されるので、結果リストの最初の要素になります。

BILINGUAL.EN: The second program makes things worse! The result is not even a list any longer, because the elements occupy the tail position of the result list and not the head position.
BILINGUAL.JA: 2番目のプログラムはさらに悪化します！結果はもはやリストですらありません。要素が結果リストの head 位置ではなく tail 位置を占めるためです。
